## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team
does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county,
including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments
drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some
households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune*
investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County:
lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than
expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago,
2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains
**only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is
yours to build.

### A real test

+---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+
| File                | What's in it                                        |
+=====================+=====================================================+
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices       |
+---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+
| `chicago_test.csv`  | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict |
|                     | them; we score you.                                 |
+---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that
sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your
test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.**

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their
portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate
uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about
*this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE,
and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of
it.

### Rules

::: callout-important
## 1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.

You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than
filtering.

## 2. Stay inside the time window

Open data from 2023–2025 only.

## 3. No leakage

Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for
a house that didn't sell?*

## 4. The outcome stays in dollars

Transform predictors, not `sale_price`.

## 5. No prices from the test fold or the future

No features built from other houses' sale prices.
:::

## Part 0: Setup (provided)

These helpers are to help you get off the ground.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)
library(spdep)
library(nngeo)
library(stats)
library(dplyr)
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}  
# helper function for calculating moran's I
# takes in all_sales and list of predictors, uses k=8 for queen weight
# example on how to call it: moran_i_cv(all_sales, predictors2)
library(sf)
library(spdep)

moran_i_cv <- function(all_sales, predictors, k = 8) {
  train <- all_sales %>%
    filter(split == "train")
  
  formula <- reformulate(
    termlabels = predictors,
    response = "sale_price"
  )
  
  cv_predictions <- cv_pred(formula, train)
  cv_residuals <- train$sale_price - cv_predictions
  
  # Extract coordinates safely whether 'train' is an sf object or standard data frame
  if (inherits(train, "sf")) {
    coords <- st_coordinates(train)
  } else if (all(c("lon", "lat") %in% colnames(train))) {
    coords <- as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")])
  } else {
    stop("`all_sales` must be an 'sf' object or contain 'lon' and 'lat' columns.")
  }
  
  neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k))
  weights <- nb2listw(
    neighbors,
    style = "W",
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  result <- moran.test(
    cv_residuals,
    weights,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Return the Moran's I statistic numeric value
  return(unname(result$estimate["Moran I statistic"]))
}

```

## Part 1: Clean and explore

Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and
how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map
of price.

### 1a. Checking for NA values and managing them

NA columns:

```{r}


library(dplyr)

train <- read_csv("data/chicago_train.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
test <- read_csv("data/chicago_train.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
colSums(is.na(train))
colSums(is.na(test))
```

There are quite a few columns with NA values. To manage this, we first

Interpolate missing `lotsize_acre` value in the `train` dataset from
checking 5 nearest neighbours:

```{r}

# extract NA row, interpolate w knn
missing_row <- all_sales |> filter(is.na(lotsize_acre)) #THIS IS A SPATIAL OBJECT
valid_rows  <- all_sales |> filter(!is.na(lotsize_acre))

# calc to the missing row and pull the 5 closest obs
knn5 <- st_nn(missing_row, valid_rows, k = 5, returnDist = FALSE, progress = FALSE)

knn5 # THIS RETURNS INDICES FROM VALID_ROWS THAT ARE NEAREST NEIGHBORA

# extrapolate index (idx) to find lotsize_acre column in original df valid_rows
lotsize_knn5 <- lapply(knn5, function(idx) {
  valid_rows$lotsize_acre[idx]
})

# Access neighbor values for the 1st missing row:
lotsize_knn5[[1]]

# ADD LOTSIZE NUMBER in the missing row in training dataset
neighbor_lotsize <- mean(lotsize_knn5[[1]], na.rm = TRUE)

all_sales <- all_sales |> 
  mutate(lotsize_acre = if_else(is.na(lotsize_acre), neighbor_lotsize, lotsize_acre))
```

Replace NA values in
`garage_size, num_fireplaces, full_basement, warmairfurnace` in both
train and test datasets with zero:

```{r}

# change NA value to zero
all_sales$garage_size[is.na(all_sales$garage_size)] <- 0
all_sales$num_fireplaces[is.na(all_sales$num_fireplaces)] <- 0
all_sales$full_basement[is.na(all_sales$full_basement)] <- 0
all_sales$warmairfurnace[is.na(all_sales$warmairfurnace)] <- 0
all_sales$num_half_baths[is.na(all_sales$num_half_baths)] <- 0
```

**Answer:** What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?

*Your answer:*

Each column for both the training and testing datasets was first
examined for NA values. Below is a list of columns displaying NA values
(and number of rows) and how it was managed:

- `lotsize_acre` (1): Lot size for that row was approximated according
  to the 5 nearest neighbours

  - Since the 5 nearest neighbors all have a lot size of 0.0717, the lot
    size for this missing value will also be approximated to 0.0717 with
    high confidence.

- `garage_size` (16): Values were changed to zero because it was assumed
  that there is no garage in the house.

- `num_half_baths` (45): Values were changed to zero because it was
  assumed that no half baths were found.

- `num_fireplaces` (412): Values were changed to zero because it was
  assumed no fireplace was found.

- `full_basement` (2): Values were changed to zero because it was
  assumed no basement was found.

- `warmairfurnace` (9): Values were changed to zero because it was
  assumed no warm air furnace was found.

### 1b: Defining market sales that are eligible for our model

The minimum value of sale_price is \$10,373, which seems plausible based
on brief market research that was carried out. All rows are kept, with
NA values replaced as mentioned above.

Market sales is defined as:

1.  **`sale_price > $1`**: To exclude any informal property transfer at
    a nominal \$1 price that is not reflective of market prices.
2.  **`sale_price < $10,000,000`:** This prediction is intended for
    normal houses. There were 3 properties about 10m that skewed the
    dataset a lot.
3.  **Any sale between 2023-2025**: Which is within the temporal limit
    of our training dataset
4.  `multisale` sales were kept because they are still reflective of a
    type of market sale. The sale price reflected is still of the
    individual property price (instead of the sum of the properties) so
    it does not inflate the data.
5.  **Average sale price per square foot \< 1855:** This was identified
    as an outlier as it was more than 3 standard deviations from the
    mean normalized Average sale price per square foot. Normalization
    was carried out to fix the skew.

```{r}

class(train)

# get census block sf object

# ggplot(blocks_sf)+

# CHOROPLETH MAP, AGGREGATED TO CENSUS BLOCKS 2020
# COUNT: total sales + median price


# st_join points to blocks. then aggregate by  block id
median_price_tracts <- st_join(train, tracts, join = st_intersects) |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  group_by(tract_ce) |> 
  summarise(
    median_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_sales  = n()

# join back to SPATIAL tracts polygons with median sale_price and counts

  left_join(median_price_tracts, by = "tract_ce") #|> 
#filter(!is.na(median_price))


hist(median_price_tracts$median_price)
# very right skewed histogram

#  the distribution of median sale price is very irregular and a jenks classification needs to be applied.
library(classInt)  # Needed to calculate Jenks breaks
library(scales)    # Needed for dollar formatting


# make jenks, EXCLUDE NA VALUES
prices_for_breaks <- na.omit(median_price_tracts$median_price)
jenks_breaks <- classIntervals(prices_for_breaks, n = 5, style = "jenks")$brks

legend_labels <- paste0(
  dollar(jenks_breaks[-length(jenks_breaks)]), 
  " - ", 
  dollar(jenks_breaks[-1])
)

# add jenks breaks into object
median_price_tracts <- median_price_tracts |> 
  mutate(
    price_class = cut(
      median_price,
      breaks = jenks_breaks,
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      labels = legend_labels
    )
  )


# extract point data for lowest and highest price (NOT MEDIAN)
extreme_points <- train %>%
  filter(sale_price == min(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE) | sale_price == max(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(type = if_else(sale_price == min(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE), "Lowest Price", "Highest Price"))


#get background tiles

library(terra)
library(ggspatial)

boundary <- st_union(tracts)


ggplot(median_price_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = price_class), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "mako",
    name = "Median Sale Price Tiers (Jenks)",
    direction = -1,
    na.value = "darkgrey"  # <-- Changes NA fills from default grey/transparent to custom grey
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = extreme_points,
    aes(color = type),
    size = 2,
    stroke = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Extremes",
    values = c("Lowest Price" = "#FF3333", "Highest Price" = "#00FF66")
  ) +
  theme_void() +

    title = "Median House Sale Prices per Census Tract"
  )
```

*A jenks classification was placed on the aggregated data of sale_price
per tract because the data is very right skewed. A jenks classification
would help to split the 5 classes in the choropleth map to reduce
variability within each class, accounting for these outliers.*

*Observations: Median sale price is the highest north of the Loop (near
Lakeview), ranging from \$2,399,000 to \$4,900,000. Median sale price
generally decreases further away from the financial district and is the
lowest in South Chicago. The*

###### Load training data and building permits

Building permits come from the City of Chicago's open-data (SODA)
endpoint for dataset `ydr8-5enu`. No app token is needed, but the API
serves 1,000 rows per request, so pages are requested with
`$limit`/`$offset` in a loop until a short page comes back. The
2023–2025 date range and the two permit types are pushed into the
`$where` clause so only the \~22k relevant rows are downloaded instead
of the full 800k+ dataset.

```{r load-permits}
permits_url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/ydr8-5enu.json"
permits_page_size <- 1000   # rows per request

permits_where <- paste(
  "issue_date >= '2023-01-01T00:00:00' AND issue_date < '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
  "AND permit_type IN ('PERMIT - NEW CONSTRUCTION', 'PERMIT - RENOVATION/ALTERATION')",
  "AND latitude IS NOT NULL AND longitude IS NOT NULL"
)

fetch_permits_page <- function(offset) {
  resp <- request(permits_url) |>
    req_url_query(
      `$select` = "id,permit_type,issue_date,latitude,longitude",
      `$where` = permits_where,
      `$order` = "id",   # a stable sort keeps page boundaries consistent between requests
      `$limit` = permits_page_size,
      `$offset` = offset
    ) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 5) |>
    req_error(body = function(resp) resp_body_string(resp)) |>
    req_perform()

  rows <- resp_body_string(resp) |>
    jsonlite::fromJSON(simplifyVector = TRUE)
  if (length(rows) == 0) return(tibble())
  as_tibble(rows)
}

permit_pages <- list()
offset <- 0
repeat {
  page <- fetch_permits_page(offset)
  permit_pages[[length(permit_pages) + 1]] <- page
  message("offset ", offset, ": ", nrow(page), " rows")
  if (nrow(page) < permits_page_size) break
  offset <- offset + permits_page_size
}

# Same column names and types as the old Building_Permits CSV read, except that
# ISSUE_DATE is already a Date (the API returns ISO 8601 timestamps, not mm/dd/yyyy).
# The API returns every field as a string, so coordinates are converted explicitly.
permits <- bind_rows(permit_pages) |>
  transmute(
    ID = as.character(id),
    PERMIT_TYPE = permit_type,
    ISSUE_DATE = as.Date(substr(issue_date, 1, 10)),
    LATITUDE = as.numeric(latitude),
    LONGITUDE = as.numeric(longitude)
  )

nrow(permits)
```

###### Filter permits to 2023–2025 new construction and renovation

The API query already applied these filters; this keeps the same checks
as a guard.

```{r filter-permits}
permits_filtered <- permits |>
  filter(
    year(ISSUE_DATE) %in% 2023:2025,
    PERMIT_TYPE %in% c("PERMIT - NEW CONSTRUCTION", "PERMIT - RENOVATION/ALTERATION"),
    !is.na(LATITUDE), !is.na(LONGITUDE)
  )

permits_sf <- permits_filtered |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(crs_m)

count(permits_filtered, PERMIT_TYPE, year = year(ISSUE_DATE))
```

Number of filtered permits within `permit_radius_m` of each sale.

```{r construction-activity}
train_sf <- all_sales |>
  st_transform(crs_m)

all_sales$construction_activity <- lengths(
  st_is_within_distance(train_sf, permits_sf, dist = permit_radius_m)
)

summary(all_sales$construction_activity)
```

## Build r5r street network

The street network comes from BBBike's Chicago OSM extract (\~100 MB,
refreshed weekly), which covers lon −88.01 to −87.40 and lat 41.64 to
42.09. Every sale falls inside that box, so the statewide Illinois PBF
(\~350 MB) isn't needed. The download is skipped if the file is already
present, and r5r caches the built network next to it, so later runs only
pay the build cost when the PBF changes.

```{r r5r-network}
r5r_dir <- "data/r5r_chicago"
dir.create(r5r_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

pbf_url <- "https://download.bbbike.org/osm/bbbike/Chicago/Chicago.osm.pbf"
pbf <- file.path(r5r_dir, basename(pbf_url))
if (!file.exists(pbf)) {
  request(pbf_url) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    req_progress() |>
    req_perform(path = pbf)
}

# # Fail early if any sale is outside the extract, which would leave it unroutable
# pbf_bbox <- c(xmin = -88.01, ymin = 41.64, xmax = -87.40, ymax = 42.09)
# stopifnot(
#   all(between(all_sales$lon, pbf_bbox["xmin"], pbf_bbox["xmax"])),
#   all(between(all_sales$lat, pbf_bbox["ymin"], pbf_bbox["ymax"]))
# )

r5r_core <- if (exists("build_network", asNamespace("r5r"))) {
  build_network(r5r_dir, verbose = FALSE)
} else {
  setup_r5(r5r_dir, verbose = FALSE)
}
```

###### Driving isochrones from the Loop

Driving-time isochrones from downtown Chicago (41.883249, -87.630944) at
the cutoffs in `isochrone_cutoffs`. Note that r5r car routing uses
free-flow speeds, so congestion isn't modelled.

###### Downtown drive time for each sale

Car travel time from downtown to each sale's own coordinates, routed
with `travel_time_matrix()`. This replaces looking each sale up in the
isochrones: the isochrones are drawn from a coarse grid and have holes
wherever a grid point can't be reached by car, which left 19 sales with
`NA`. Routing each sale snaps it to the nearest drivable road instead.

```{r downtown-drive-time}
downtown <- data.frame(id = "downtown", lat = 41.883249, lon = -87.630944)

# Many sales share coordinates, so route each unique location once.
# r5r needs an `id` column, which is renamed so it doesn't clash with all_sales$id
sale_pts <- all_sales |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(lon, lat) |>
  mutate(pt_id = as.character(row_number()))

downtown_tt <- travel_time_matrix(
  r5r_core,
  origins = downtown,
  destinations = rename(sale_pts, id = pt_id),
  mode = "CAR",
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2023-10-04 08:00:00"),
  max_trip_duration = 90,
  progress = FALSE
)

all_sales <- all_sales |>
  select(-any_of("downtown_drive_time")) |>
  left_join(sale_pts, by = c("lon", "lat")) |>
  left_join(select(downtown_tt, pt_id = to_id, downtown_drive_time = travel_time_p50), by = "pt_id") |>
  select(-pt_id)

summary(all_sales$downtown_drive_time)
```

###### Home-to-work distance from LODES OD data

Straight-line (Euclidean) distance in meters between the centroids of
each OD pair's home block (`h_geocode`) and work block (`w_geocode`).

```{r od-distance}
# LODES8 2023 Illinois OD, all jobs (JT00), all workers (S000). "main" keeps pairs where
# both home and work are in Illinois; lehdr caches the ~30 MB download.
lodes_args <- list(
  state = "il", year = 2023, version = "LODES8",
  lodes_type = "od", job_type = "JT00", segment = "S000",
  agg_geo = "block", state_part = "main", use_cache = TRUE
)

od_raw <- tryCatch(
  do.call(grab_lodes, lodes_args),
  error = function(e) {
    if (!grepl("outside the valid range", conditionMessage(e))) stop(e)
    # lehdr 1.2.0 hard-codes LODES8 years as 2002-2022 even though the 2023 release exists.
    # Reproduce what grab_lodes() does for that file: same URL, cache path and column types.
    message("lehdr rejected year 2023; downloading the LODES8 file directly instead")
    lodes_url <- "https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/il/od/il_od_main_JT00_2023.csv.gz"
    lodes_cache <- tools::R_user_dir("lehdr", which = "cache")
    dir.create(lodes_cache, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    lodes_file <- file.path(lodes_cache, paste0("lodes8_", basename(lodes_url)))
    if (!file.exists(lodes_file)) {
      request(lodes_url) |> req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> req_perform(path = lodes_file)
    }
    read_csv(lodes_file, col_types = cols(w_geocode = "c", h_geocode = "c", createdate = "c")) |>
      mutate(year = 2023L, state = "IL")
  }
)

# Keep only pairs with both blocks in Cook County (FIPS 17031), matching the old CSV.
od <- od_raw |>
  # Geocodes stay character so the 15-digit block GEOIDs keep full precision
  mutate(across(c(w_geocode, h_geocode), as.character)) |>
  filter(str_starts(h_geocode, "17031"), str_starts(w_geocode, "17031")) |>
  select(w_geocode, h_geocode, year, S000) |>
  mutate(S000 = as.integer(S000))

# LODES 2023 uses 2020 census blocks; OD workplaces fall in Cook and DuPage
blocks <- blocks(state = "IL", county = c("Cook", "DuPage"), year = 2020) |>
  select(GEOID20) |>
  st_transform(crs_m)

# Point-on-surface guarantees the point falls inside irregularly shaped blocks
block_xy <- blocks |>
  st_point_on_surface() |>
  mutate(x = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
         y = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

od <- od |>
  select(-any_of("distance")) |>
  left_join(rename(block_xy, w_x = x, w_y = y), by = c("w_geocode" = "GEOID20")) |>
  left_join(rename(block_xy, h_x = x, h_y = y), by = c("h_geocode" = "GEOID20")) |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((w_x - h_x)^2 + (w_y - h_y)^2)) |>
  select(-w_x, -w_y, -h_x, -h_y)

summary(od$distance)
```

###### Average distance to work by home block

The average distance to work of the residents of each home block. The
mean is weighted by `S000` (the number of workers in each OD row), so it
is the average per worker. Use `mean()` instead if you want an
unweighted average across OD rows.

```{r avg-distance-by-home}
home_distance <- od |>
  group_by(h_geocode) |>
  summarise(
    average_distance_to_work = weighted.mean(distance, S000, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_workers = sum(S000),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summary(home_distance$average_distance_to_work)

# Block-group fallback for small blocks with no LODES residents (GEOID's first 12 digits)
home_bg_distance <- od |>
  mutate(h_bg = substr(h_geocode, 1, 12)) |>
  group_by(h_bg) |>
  summarise(
    bg_average_distance_to_work = weighted.mean(distance, S000, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

###### Average distance to work for each sale

Each sale is assigned to the census block it falls in and matched to
that block's resident average. Sales in small blocks with no
LODES-recorded residents fall back to their block group's average
instead.

```{r average-distance-to-work}
train_sf <- all_sales |>
  st_transform(crs_m)

train_blocks <- train_sf |>
  st_join(blocks, join = st_within) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(id, GEOID20)

all_sales <- all_sales |>
  select(-any_of("average_distance_to_work")) |>
  left_join(train_blocks, by = "id") |>
  left_join(select(home_distance, h_geocode, average_distance_to_work),
            by = c("GEOID20" = "h_geocode")) |>
  mutate(h_bg = substr(GEOID20, 1, 12)) |>
  left_join(home_bg_distance, by = "h_bg") |>
  mutate(average_distance_to_work = coalesce(average_distance_to_work, bg_average_distance_to_work)) |>
  select(-GEOID20, -h_bg, -bg_average_distance_to_work)

summary(all_sales$average_distance_to_work)
mean(is.na(all_sales$average_distance_to_work))
```

#### 2b.i Baseline

The baseline model (from the original training dataset) will first be
built:

```{r}
predictors_baseline <- c(
  "year",
  "sale_qrt",
  "is_multisale",
  "building_000sf",
  "building_age",
  "lotsize_acre",
  "num_bedrooms",
  "num_full_baths",
  "num_half_baths",
  "num_fireplaces",
  "garage_size",
  "central_air",
  "one_story",
  "full_basement",
  "finished_basement",
  "brick_stone_ext",
  "warmairfurnace"
)

#build baseline model
f1 <- reformulate(termlabels = predictors_baseline, response = "sale_price")
m1 <- lm(f1, data = train_df)
summary(m1)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m1", added = "Baseline",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f1, train_df),
          moran = moran_i_cv(train_df, predictors_baseline),
          notes = "Original, untransformed variables")

#model_log <- model_log[-1, ]  # to remove row
model_log
```

The baseline model has an adjusted R-squared of 0.66 meaning that it can
explain 66% of variance in the training dataset, which is pretty good.
The CV RMSE is \$297k, meaning that the model is \$297k off from actual
(unseen) data.

```{r}
f2 <- reformulate(termlabels = predictors2, response = "sale_price")
m2 <- lm(f2, data = train_df)
#summary(m2)


model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "log-transformed building_000sf",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, train_df),
         # moran = moran_i_cv(train_df, predictors2),
          notes = "Due to building_000sf right skewness")

#model_log <- model_log[-2, ]  # to remove row
model_log
```

The log-transformation increased the RMSE. We will use the normal
variable instead.

No change.

**2) Adding categories for our categorical variables (that are not
binary and have multiple categories)**

This includes
`year, sale_qrt, num_bedrooms, num_full_baths, num_half_baths, num_fireplaces, garage_size.`

We will test each one by one, using `as.factor()` and logging each
factorization as a separate model log.

Now that factorization is complete, we will test each subsequent
transformation against previous model. If the RMSE is lowered, the
transformation is kept. If the RMSE worsens, it is removed.

**3) Squared term for building age**

The scatterplot showed some bending for sale price against building age:

```{r}


ggplot(train_df, aes(x = building_age, y = sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_smooth(#method = "lm", formula = y ~ x ,   #REMOVE LM TO PLOT SMOOTHING LINE INSTEAD
    color = "red",
    se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = paste("Sale Price vs Building Age"),
    x = "Building Age",
    y = "Sale Price"
  )
```

This is to be expected given that home values tend to drop with physical
depreciation. But with much older buildings with historic charm/major
renovations, that decline either flattens out or reverses.

We add a squared term to account for this bend in the line:

```{r}


predictors11 <- c(
  "year",                      # factorized
  "sale_qrt",                  # factorized
  "is_multisale",
  "building_000sf",
  "building_age",
  "I(building_age^2)",         # add squared term
  "lotsize_acre",
  "num_bedrooms",              # factorized
  "num_full_baths",
  "num_half_baths",            
  "num_fireplaces",            # factorized            
  "garage_size",               # factorized
  "central_air",
  "one_story",
  "full_basement",
  "finished_basement",
  "brick_stone_ext",
  "warmairfurnace"
)

f11 <- reformulate(termlabels = predictors11, response = "sale_price")

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model   = "m11",
    added   = "m10 + squared building_age",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f11, train_df),
    moran = moran_i_cv(train_df, predictors11),
    notes   = "new predictor: I(building_age^2)"
  )

print(model_log, n=40)

#model_log <- model_log[-(13), ]
```

RMSE improved!

```{r}
train_sf <- all_sales %>%
```

```{r}
baseline_resid <- train_sf$sale_price - cv_pred(f_baseline, train_sf)
final_resid <- train_sf$sale_price - cv_pred(f_final, train_sf)

residual_maps <- bind_rows(
  train_sf %>% mutate(model = "Baseline", residual = baseline_resid),
  train_sf %>% mutate(model = "Final", residual = final_resid)
)

# THERE IS HIGH SKEW
summary(residual_maps$residual)
quantile(residual_maps$residual, c(.01, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .99), na.rm = TRUE)


# 
library(scales)

ggplot(residual_maps %>% arrange(abs(residual))) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = residual), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "grey85", high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    trans = pseudo_log_trans(sigma = median(abs(residual_maps$residual))),   # sigma ~ a "typical small" residual in $
    labels = label_dollar(),
    breaks = c(-1e6, -1e5, -1e4, 0, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6),
    name = "Residual\n(actual - predicted)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The final RMSE is 271036. Our baseline model was 297569. The final model
predictions improved on unseen data by \~\$26k. The final RMSE was still
higher than previous models we tested on, indicating that it is
predicting unseen data a little worse. However, standard
cross-validation does not account for spatial factors - since Moran's I
is better, it indicates the model has better captured spatial patterns
in the data.

The transformations of the variables, especially the addition of the
squared variables helped the most.

The variables that disappointed us the most is actually not included in
the model. It includes things like flood score, which we thought might
be a powerful variable given that Chicago experiences high levels of
flooding.

## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays

**4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high
or too low there, and why do you think so?

**4B.** Assessors judge their work with the **ratio** of predicted value
to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its
owner over-taxed. Does your model's ratio differ by neighborhood income?
Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to "The Tax
Divide."

```{r}

summary(residual_maps$residual)
hist(residual_maps$residual)

```

*Your answers:*

First of all, we had to (pseudo) log-transform the scale because based
on the summary of the residuals distribution, it is very skewed. To
interpret the map:

1.  Grey: model is accurate.
2.  Red: model is underpredicting. At extreme values of red, model is
    **severely** underpredicting.
3.  Blue: model is overpredicting. At extreme values of blue, model is
    **severely** overpredicting.

Our final model fails the worst at predicting house prices that are
actually very high, especially those near the Loop. The model is
guessing too low. We think this is because it is more difficult to
predict for the range of a “very expensive” house, which is much larger
than that of an average-priced house. Moreover, we assumed that a fixed
effect spatial feature (e.g. distance to the Loop) would not need to be
included in our model because it would be collinear with other similar
"spatial" features like downtown drive time, which would have reflected
similar patterns. In further iterations, we should include distance to
the Loop.

**Ratio**

```{r}
train_sf <- train_sf %>%
  mutate(
    predicted_price = cv_pred(f_final, .),
    pred_ratio = predicted_price / sale_price
  )

# summary statistics of the ratio
summary(train_sf$pred_ratio)

# percentage of sales predicted within +/- 10% of actual price
mean(between(train_sf$pred_ratio, 0.90, 1.10), na.rm = TRUE)
```

Our model’s ratio, with a median of 0.998 differs by neighborhood
income. The maximum ratio is 67 which is very high - this indicates
predicted price was way overpredicted of the actual sale price.

However the highest ratio of 67 means that those houses are over-valued.
**This means that lower-income neighborhoods face disproportionate
property tax-burden compared to higher-income neighborhoods.**
Conversely, luxury homes in higher-income areas often sell at premium
prices that standard linear models under-predict (ratios below 1.0, like
the 1st quartile of 0.743), leaving wealthier homeowners under-taxed.

This imbalance mirrors the core finding of The Tax Divide. Algorithmic
and traditional assessment models routinely over-assess low-value
properties while under-assessing high-value properties, creating a
regressive tax structure.

In part 1, we cleaned out houses that cost over around \$1800 per square
foot, houses less than \$20,000 and houses over \$10 million. When we
examined the standard deviation for price per square foot in the
training dataset, three standard deviations away from the mean was 1800.
We cleaned out 5 upper outliers this way that seemed way too far from
the rest of our data set to accurately contribute to the model.
Filtering out the low-end sales under \$20k created an artificial price
floor forcing the model to over-predict low-income home values that were
outside of our model range. Simultaneously, removing luxury outliers
(\>\$1800/sqft and \>\$10m) capped top-end predictions which led to
under-assessment in these high-income neighborhoods. By trimming these
extreme data anchors, the cleaning actually caused regressivity across
both ends of the income spectrum.

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1.  **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to
    ŷ.
2.  **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn
    them about?

*Your answer:*

`violentcrime_660ft`: Holding all other structural, location, and
quadratic terms constant, each additional violent crime reported within
660 feet of a home is associated with an estimated linear decrease of
**\$3,694.90** in sale price.

If we were to hand this model in to the Assessor, we would warn them
about a number of things.

(**1) T**he model exhibits significant residual error and spatial bias.
With an RMSE of \$\\\$271,036\$, individual property valuations can be
off by hundreds of thousands of dollars. Furthermore, a Moran's I of
0.270 indicates strong positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning the
model's errors are geographically clustered—it will systematically
over-value or under-value entire neighborhoods rather than spreading
errors randomly. Additionally, sparse extreme features create
unrealistic coefficient swings (e.g., 12 bedrooms reducing predicted
value by over \$1.49M and 1 fireplace having a negative coefficient),
making the model vulnerable to edge-case properties.

**(2)** There are many factors that influence a house’s sale price. We
were able to explore many factors in this exercise through open-sources
alone. However, there are a lot of proprietary datasets that are locked
behind a paywall (i.e. GreatSchools for school ratings and performance).
If the Assessor wants even further analysis done on predicting house
sale prices, they may want to consider additional datasets.

**(3)** On the other hand, using too many factors could add unintended
noise to the model. Given more time, we would test both more and fewer
features to see their impact on our model.
